title: ETFs vs Mutual Funds vs Stocks: Which Should Beginners Choose?

scenes.chapterTitle: Intro: most stocks lose to cash
scenes.badge: US stocks that failed to beat Treasury bills over their lifetime

chips.text: Not a crash. Their whole life.

scenes.text: Here's a number that surprises most new investors. A finance professor studied every US stock from nineteen twenty six to twenty sixteen, and fifty eight percent of them failed to beat one month Treasury bills over their entire life. That's basically cash. So if you pick one stock at random, the odds are not on your side. In this video, I'll compare the three main ways beginners own stocks: single stocks, mutual funds and ETFs. We'll look at how they're bought, what they cost, how they're taxed, and a simple way to decide.

scenes.title: One share or a basket
scenes.sub: A stock is one company. A fund holds many.
scenes.text: Let's start simple. A stock is a small piece of one company. If that company does well, your share can rise. If it struggles, your share falls, and nothing else is there to cushion it. A fund is different. It pools money from lots of investors and buys a basket of many stocks or bonds. Mutual funds and ETFs are both funds. The main difference between them isn't what they own. It's the wrapper: how you buy them, how they're priced, and how they're taxed.

scenes.chapterTitle: Stocks, mutual funds and ETFs in plain English

items.name: ETF

items.name: Index or active
items.desc: Follow a list, or a manager picks

scenes.text: Here are the three side by side. A single stock is part of one company, and you can buy or sell it whenever the market is open. A mutual fund holds a basket, but you buy it at one price per day, calculated after the market closes. An exchange traded fund, or ETF, also holds a basket, but it trades all day like a stock. And both kinds of fund can be either index funds, which follow a fixed list, or active funds, where a manager picks. Same baskets, different wrapper.

scenes.chapterTitle: The problem with picking single stocks

chips.text: A fund owns the few big winners

footer.text: Finding the winners early is the hard part

scenes.text: A long study of US stocks found that out of nearly twenty six thousand US stocks, just four point three percent, about one thousand ninety two companies, created all of the stock market's net wealth above Treasury bills. Only eighty six stocks produced half of it. The market's long term gains came from a small group of huge winners. A broad fund owns those winners automatically, along with everything else. If you hold a handful of single stocks, you need to find the winners early. That's the hard part.

scenes.text: Now, how you actually buy them. With a mutual fund, you place an order and everyone gets the same price, set once after the market closes. You can usually invest an exact dollar amount, which makes automatic monthly investing easy, though many funds ask for a minimum first investment. An ETF or a stock has a live price while the market is open. You buy shares, and many brokers now offer fractional shares, so you can invest smaller amounts. Same basket, different way to buy it. Check your own broker for minimums and fractional shares.

scenes.chapterTitle: Where investors are moving their money
scenes.text: Here's where investors are putting their money. At the end of twenty twenty five, US mutual funds still held about thirty one point four trillion dollars, according to the Investment Company Institute. ETFs held about thirteen point four trillion. But the direction is clear. In twenty twenty five, ETFs took in a record of about one and a half trillion dollars of new money, while mutual funds saw about six hundred ninety two billion dollars flow out. Mutual funds are still the bigger pile, especially in retirement plans, but money is moving toward ETFs.

footer.text: The money is moving toward ETFs

scenes.chapterTitle: The tax difference most beginners miss

chips.text: No difference inside an IRA or 401(k)

footer.text: Source: Morningstar data via State Street

scenes.text: This next part is the difference most beginners miss: taxes. When a fund sells holdings at a profit, it can pass that gain to you as a capital gains distribution, and you may owe tax on it even if you never sold a share. According to Morningstar data reported by State Street, only seven percent of ETFs paid a capital gain in twenty twenty five, compared with fifty two percent of mutual funds. This matters in a regular taxable account. Inside a retirement account, like an IRA or a four oh one k, these payouts aren't taxed each year.

scenes.chapterTitle: What each one costs per year
scenes.text: What about cost? The Investment Company Institute says that in twenty twenty five, index stock mutual funds charged an average of just zero point zero five percent a year. Index stock ETFs averaged zero point one four percent. All stock mutual funds, including active ones, averaged zero point four zero percent. And a single stock has no yearly fee at all, but you carry all the risk. Notice the bigger lesson here. The gap between index and active funds is larger than the gap between ETFs and mutual funds. Low cost index funds exist in both wrappers.

scenes.text: So which fits which beginner? A mutual fund can suit you if you like automatic investing in exact dollar amounts, and it's often what a workplace plan offers. An ETF can suit a regular taxable account, because of the lower tax payouts, and you can buy it at almost any broker. Single stocks can make sense as a small slice you're willing to lose while you learn. And if your four oh one k only offers mutual funds, that's fine. Look for the low cost index options on the menu. Match the wrapper to the account.

items.text: Broad index fund as the core
ETF or mutual fund: what fits
Single stocks: a small slice only

scenes.text: Here's a simple checklist. One, decide which account you're using, a taxable account or a retirement account, because that changes how much taxes matter. Two, consider a broad, low cost index fund as the core, so you own the whole market instead of guessing. Three, compare expense ratios, the yearly cost. Four, pick the ETF or mutual fund version based on your broker, your account, and how you like to invest. And five, if you want single stocks, keep them a small slice. Then think about your own goals and timeline.

scenes.title: Own the basket first
scenes.sub: The wrapper matters less than cost and spread
scenes.text: Here's the big idea. For most beginners, the question isn't really ETF versus mutual fund. It's one company versus the whole basket, and high cost versus low cost. History shows that most single stocks lag cash over their lifetime, while a broad fund holds the rare winners for you. ETFs tend to be more tax efficient in a taxable account, and mutual funds are great for automatic investing. Either way, all of them can drop in a bad market. This is education, not financial advice.

youtube.title: ETFs vs Mutual Funds vs Stocks: Which Should Beginners Choose?
youtube.summary: 58% of US stocks failed to beat Treasury bills over their lifetime. This is a plain-English comparison of the three main ways beginners own stocks: single stocks, mutual funds and ETFs. We cover how each is bought and priced, where investors moved their money in 2025, the capital gains tax difference between ETFs and mutual funds, what each costs per year, which one fits which kind of account, and a 5-step beginner checklist.
youtube.details:
Numbers mentioned (checked November 2026):
- 58% of US common stocks failed to beat one-month Treasury bills over their lifetime; about 1,092 companies (4.3% of nearly 26,000 stocks) accounted for all net wealth creation above T-bills, and 86 stocks for half of it, 1926 to 2016 (Hendrik Bessembinder, 'Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills?', via ASU W. P. Carey, Sept 2018).
- US mutual funds about $31.4 trillion and ETFs about $13.4 trillion in net assets at year-end 2025 (ICI 2026 Fact Book, as reported by Walnut, Oct 2026). ETF net share issuance a record ~$1.5 trillion in 2025 (ICI via PlanSponsor, Apr 2026); US mutual funds about $692 billion of outflows in 2025 (State Street, Feb 2026).
- 7% of ETFs vs 52% of mutual funds paid a capital gains distribution in 2025 (Morningstar data, reported by State Street Global Advisors, Feb 2026).
- Average yearly costs in 2025: index equity mutual funds 0.05%, index equity ETFs 0.14%, all equity mutual funds 0.40% (ICI, Trends in the Expenses and Fees of Funds, 2025, March 2026).
- Capital gains distributions are generally not taxed each year inside tax-advantaged retirement accounts. Tax rules depend on your situation and country; this video uses US examples.
